messages.content:
Who was the best debater among American Presidents?
Sarah Smith
I remember watching Obama’s “Horses and Bayonets” quip. That’s the exact moment he won the election in my mind.


Michael Brown
I beieve that it was in 2008, the 150th Anniversary of the Lincoln-Douglas debates that the State of Illinois, in partnership with public television, created a series of re-enactments of the famous debates.
Apparently, enough of the text was written down or remembered by eyewitnesses that in modern times the following could be done:
Two actors were chosen at a time and were able to restate — more or less word for word— what Abe Lincoln and Stephen Douglas actually said during those debates. And those were REAL debates, not just joint press conferences. Here was the format:
One of the two candidates, chosen at random, got up and spoke for an hour.
The other canidate then spoke for ninety minutes.
Finally, the first candidate got a half hour “rebuttal” speech.
The result? These broadcasts showed these two candidates—Douglas and Lincoln—to be articulate, intelligent, eloquent, and utterly brilliant in responding to each other. They had eloquence and mastery of the English language that seems to go well beyond anyone we’ve seen lately, even Obama. And these two could “go for the jugular” and score very big points, without ever lowering themselves to the vulgarisms of Trump.
(Historical note: the Lincoln-Douglas debates occurred in 1858, when Lincoln and Douglas were running for US Senator from Illinois. Douglas won, but the debates were published in newspapers all over America, making Lincoln nationally famous. That helped him to win the Republican Presidential nomination in 1860 when — amazingly — his Democratic opponent was none other than Stephen A. Douglas, the same man he’d lost the Senate race to! But this time, in 1860, Lincoln won.)
In short, I would go with Abraham Lincoln. I doubt it would be even close. The greatest American orator/Senator was Daniel Webster, who might have given Lincoln a run for his money, but Webster was never elected president, though he wanted to be.
Among later presidents, the only one who might have come close to giving Lincoln a challenge, I think, would be Franklin D. Roosevelt. His way with words, demonstrated in his Fireside Chats, was amazing. In one speech after another, he would turn attacks on him to his advantage, rather than wilting, as later Democrats sometimes have done. When criticized by the bankers on Wall Street, FDR did not fold but said “I welcome their hatred!” and then made it clear to the American public why that was a good thing.
Lincoln and FDR… perhaps not coincidentally, they may also be the two greatest American presidents in general, not just as debaters.
In a real, all-out debate, I don’t think any of our other presidents, or presidential candidates, would stand a chance against either Lincoln or FDR.


Robert Green · 
Lincoln’s second innagural was eloquence.


Michael Brown
 That is true also.


Jason Clark 
I believe it’s the greatest speech ever given by an American president.


Kevin Turner
Debating and oratory are two different things.
My vote would go to James Madison. He understood debate. His arguments and papers during the debate process for the US Constitution showed great talent and insight.
He could deconstruct arguments brick by brick and construct his own arguments brick by brick. He had a great sense of logic and human nature.
He was certainly not the greatest orator. That would go to Lincoln. But he was the best debater.


Raj Patel
Since when?
I ask that because most US Presidents are dead.
Out of the ones who are still living, personally, I’d say President Obama. This is based on what I know of him, mainly his reputation, as I only really started following American Politics when Trump got involved, not that I had taken no notice previously. Its just that Obama concentrated more on running the USA than Trump did. Trump concentrated on his social media presence and golf more.
I have seen clips of Obama answering questions and debating and, from what I can tell, he ‘knew his stuff.’ Although there seemed to be a fair few ‘erms’ and ‘pauses’ with Obama. But I think that was him thinking what the best way to deliver the answer would be.
Although I have never had the honour of meeting him he seems, and much of what I have read certainly backs this up, a genuine, nice, friendly guy.
I remember one youtube clip I saw when some Journalist Students were on a trip to the White House Press room and one of the Obama officials was giving a speech and then the students (who didn’t look thrilled and seemed quite bored) would ask questions. The atmosphere changed when Obama strolled in and said ‘I head you guys were here and thought I’d just pop along and say hi and answer any questions.’ The atmosphere changed from ‘When do I get out of here’ to ‘OH WOW OBAMA’s HERE.’
I’m not saying he did not have faults, nor am I saying I agreed with all his policies (although it was mainly just the major ones made it to the UK news) however, when it comes to debates - he’s the guy you want on your team.


Steve Black


Abraham Lincoln. His debates with Stephen Douglas in the run up for the US Senator from Illinois election in 1858 became a national media event. This series of debates articulated the two parties positions on slavery.
It won Lincoln the national recognition to win the presidency two years later.
It convinced the Southern plantation class that Lincoln's election would lead to the end of their theft of human labor.


Richard Anderson
Lincoln probably since we have an extensive record of his debates. Others are harder to judge since the best legislative debaters did not win the presidency.
In addition you have people actually capable of debating substance vs. scoring memorized scorches like “you are no Jack Kennedy”. Someone took votes on the JFK/Nixon debates, and the ones who listened on the radio thought Nixon won, but the ones who watched on TV said JFK did, possibly influenced by JFK’s good looks or Nixon’s heavy sweating. Which would you say was “best” when these factors are considered?



Chris Lewis
None.
Why?
During these debates none of the candidates demonstrated they were deserving of my vote - including those I did eventually vote for. I repeat that -NONE!
Regrettably- American Presidential debates have degenerated into a series of gotcha questions and sound bites or the even worse “Citizen” questions which are essentially- “My hand is open for a bribe. What are you going to put in it?” type question.
Since the Reagan/Carter debates I learned absolutely nothing about the Candidates thinking and approach that I did not already know. Thus the debates turn into a horserace type event which I find completely uninteresting.
A much better one would be a variation on the cross-ex. One candidate is given the lead-a set time to propose what he intends to do as President. The opposing candidate then gets a set time for direct cross-ex after which he gives a rebuttal of the lead with a cross- ex by the lead at the end of his rebuttal. Both candidates are then allowed to give a summary.
Note that this really requires two debates so each has the opportunity as the lead
You do have to set a time limit for each and you have to enforce it - cutting off of microphones for example. In my own debating experience the timekeeper would stand up and show you when you had one minute remaining. At the end of that minute you are done - whether you are finished with your presentation or not.
The advantages are
No moderators! This alone would be a huge improvement over the travesties we currently have to endure every four years.
It limits the opportunity for relentless sound bites and promises that mean exactly zero and tell you exactly zero. The fact that he is subject to a direct cross-examination by his opponent means that you are going to get real information as to his intent , how he approaches issues and how well he thinks under pressure- both critical to the performance of any President.








Michael Brown
I’m going to cheat on this. Technically, the Lincoln-Douglas debates of 1858 occurred during an Illinois senatorial election between Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas. (The latter won, although according to Doris Kearns Goodwin this was only because there was no popular-vote election for senators in Illinois at the time.)
But two years later, the same two candidates emerged as the Republican and Democratic candidates for President of the USA! The L-D debates, then, although technically “senatorial,” not “presidential” debates, were in fact the major debates between candidates leading up to a presidential election.
The L-D debates were far closer to a real debate than anything we’ve had in the modern era, which are really just joint press conferences, in which some interaction is allowed between the candidates.
But in the L-D debates, the two speakers had to speak at great length and do detailed analysis of the other candidate’s remarks. And that, both Lincoln and Douglas did brilliantly… speaking to the common man but giving lengthy, detailed analysis.
Of the two, I think Lincoln did the more brilliant job, but Stephen Douglas was formidable as well.
As they say, “They just don’t make them like that anymore.”


Emily Davis
Bill Clinton was a master of connection. You watching him through a box in your home while he’s in a room thousands of miles away from you talking to millions of people and he makes you feel like he’s just sitting across from you in your living room having a casual conversation. I’m pretty sure he used some sort of witchcraft.


Alan Wilson
Obama had some great moments debating. Against Hillary when he was seeking the DNC nomination he was outstanding at times. I also think getting beaten by mitt Romney in the first presidential debate that you had fired him up. Obama came out in the second debate like a prizefighter looking for a knockout. I was not an Obama fan, I didn’t vote for him. But I saw how good the guy could be.
I don’t think either of these opponents or anyone really impressive to go up against him. But he showed his a game was one of the best we’ve ever seen on the presidential stage.
Ronald Reagan was also very impressive. Not because of his content, but his ability to be in control of the situation. He made Walter Mondale look horrible. Reagan acting skills lent them to his great performance.
it’s hard to gauge anybody pre-television era on how they performed. Most people know from history books that Lincoln was considered a skilled debater but the arena has changed so much since he was debating. I imagine Theodore Roosevelt would’ve been a ferocious person to square off against. Right or wrong, going against TR, You would likely be in for the fight of your political career.
Donald Trump is also a very skilled debater because he understands how to work the crowd. Again right or wrong he’s usually in control of the situation. That makes it tough to go against him. It’s frightening honestly.


Martin P. Evans
I am not an expert on this topic, but Lincoln stands out. Otherwise, a couple that have not been mentioned yet would be Theodore Roosevelt (a sharp communicator who connected well with audiences and could work the press) and Ronald Reagan (who leveraged his acting ability to land jabs and make convincing points and also had the experience in how to prepare for a debate or speech).


Lisa Hall
Clinton’s the only one I can remember who I don’t think ever lost a debate. Reagan was crushed by Mondale in the first debate in ‘84 and it led to a small bounce for Mondale that Reagan crushed for good with his legendary joke in the 2nd debate. Obama was pushed around by Romney in the first debate in 2012 which gave Romney a bounce, which Obama then killed with strong performances in the 2nd and 3rd debates. But Clinton had debates against 2 candidates in ‘92 (one a sitting president), and then with Dole in ‘96 and never lost once.
But if we take out the bad first debates of Reagan in ‘84 and Obama in ‘12, they might be best.




Daniel Cohen
In the late 1850s, Abraham Lincoln famously held a series of debates (on slavery and states’ rights) with Stephen A. Douglas, a powerful Senator from Illinois (Lincoln’s home state, too) who later ran for President (and lost) against Lincoln. The Lincoln-Douglas Debates, as history calls them, thrust private citizen Lincoln into the national arena, holding his own (or besting) Douglas who was known as one of the nation’s most gifted orators. Whether or not this makes Lincoln “the best debater,” it did help make him President.


Anthony Rossi
Lincoln was supposedly an awesome speaker. JFK also gave great speeches. The greatest speaker of the modern era, however, was Ronald Reagan. Tip O’Neill who knew JFK very well and also knew President Reagan recalled having a pretty heated exchange with Reagan on January 28 1986. He remembered leaving the White House in an angry mood. Later that day the Space Shuttle Challenger exploded, killing everyone on board. O’NEILL recalled Reagan’s beautiful, healing address to the nation and commented that Reagan was the greatest speaker he’d ever heard and that his ability to give a speech surpassed JFK’s.
Karen Miller
Perot was also an amazing debater. He knew policy very very well and was hilarious. It’s just impossible to win as an independent in a two party system.
Paul Taylor
Disagree. Perot's campaign began to flounder once he became a serious candidate and the media stopped giving him darling status. He really struggled once he was pressed to get specific on his policy positions. He tended to get pretty testy, and was frankly pretty thin-skinned. Didn't help that the public thought Gore wrecked him in the NAFTA debate.
People remember him more fondly than he really deserves, because nostalgia is rosy. He wasn't that spectacular of a candidate once you got below "free trade bad" levels of policy positions.




Frank Mitchell
The question is, “Who was or is the best presidential debater of all time?” The question doesn’t limit debates to those between presidential candidates. So I nominate
James Madison
Madison was a key figure in the debate over whether to ratify the US Constitution. Can you imagine what America would be like now if the Constitution had not been ratified? A world power? Or a loose confederacy of slave and free states?
Madison was one of the three authors of The Federalist Papers, a key part of the debate which remains in print today. And Madison was a key participant in Virginia’s ratification convention. See “The Federalist Papers and ratification debates” section of James Madison - Wikipedia. Madison wrote 29 of the 85 original essays. This was surely an important form of debate then.
The anti-Federalist aren’t much remembered today. But they were strong in Virginia and New York. If Virginia didn’t ratify, New York probably would not. And then the Constitution would fail. And the anti-Federalists were led in Virginia by Patrick Henry. The Wikipedia article says Madison successfully matched Henry, meting emotional appeals with rational arguments. And Virginia ratified the Constitution.
Pretty good results in debates that were as important for America as later debates about slavery.


Gary Roberts
James Garfield. The man had a reputation as a great orator years before he was President. It is said that while he was in the Senate sometimes he would speak as many as 40 times a day. Then during the 1880 Republican Convention there were three contenders. Ulysses S. Grant who had already served two terms, James Blaine of Maine, and the younger brother of William Tecumseh Sherman, John Sherman. As the convention dragged on, mainly because there were three very viable candidates, there was some speculation that perhaps Garfield would also make a good one. But he didn't seem interested. Then John Sherman asked Garfield to give Sherman's nominating speech at the convention. Garfield agreed, but only reluctantly. Right there is good indication of Garfield's ability to give a good speech. You generally want the guy giving your nomination speech at the Republican Convention to either be enthusiastic about the sort of President you would make or that they could give one helluva of a speech even if they weren't.
The only problem was Garfield was so lacking in enthusiasm that up to the very day of the nominating speech, he had yet to write a single world in support of Sherman. But not surprisingly, the man Grant recruited to give his nomination speech was also a great orator. So much so he worked the crowd of Republicans at the Convention into a frenzy, including Garfield. The man's speech so inspired Garfield that when it was his turn to speak he brought the entire floor to its feet in applause. The speech was so impressive, some delegates made attempts to get him to throw his own hat into the political ring. But Garfield refused. Then the balloting began. That day the entire convention voted thirty times without a clear winner. The voting dragged on for days. Then on the 34th ballot, 16 from Wisconsin voted for Garfield. He immediately rose for a point of order asking if a man could even be nominated if he didn't wish to. The chair refused to acknowledge the point and the balloting continued. With Garfield now included in the nomination process the standing changed but not enough to declare a winner so another vote was ordered. This time Garfield won 399 votes, which was more than enough to nominated him as the Republican candidate. The man never wanted the Presidency and he didn't even campaign as the Republican candidate. Yet, he still won the highest office in the land and it was all because of an imprompt speech he gave without a hint of preparation before the event.
Therefore, President James A. Garfield was the best orator out of all the men who have ever served in that office.


John Carter
 Probably Abraham Lincoln and James Garfield were the two best. Today candidates have to have at least some basic debating skills, because we’ve made public debates part of the campaigning process.
Diane King
I think Bernie is cut throat. It ticks me off that I learn more about candidates through same party debates than when they’re debating the actual opponent. Once they’re that far, they’re just talking heads
Mary Sullivan
My favorite clip of his is when he said “I wrote the damn bill!” I don’t remember the context. Never been a Sanders fan but that was a mic drop moment.
Carlos Diaz
There was a saying about how for every politician flip flopping on an issue, you can find a video of Bernie arguing for where they eventually landed. He’s on the right side of issues.
I loved that mic drop moment you mentioned though!




Eric Hoffman
I don't k ow if he was the best but Ronald Reagan was a very talented debater and speaker.


Philip Stone


There are several interesting possible matchups here but for me there’s one that would top them all. A debate between the two greatest politicians ever to live in the White House. The event would begin with the moderator’s opening. He/she would bring the two men out about like this:
Ladies and gentlemen, we ask you to hold all applause except for now as we introduce the candidates.
The Republican candidate, Congressman Abraham Lincoln.
And the Democratic candidate, Governor Franklin Roosevelt.
Imagine, a debate between these two men. FDR’s warm speaking voice would probably beat Honest Abe (whose voice was said to be uneven and a bit quavery) but I do not believe that alone would decide the election. I’m also certain that Roosevelt’s physical handicap would not have hurt him with viewers/voters. Between Lincoln’s folksy anecdotes and Roosevelt’s homey metaphors for policies, the discussion would be anything but boring. Best of all, the country would win no matter which candidate was victorious.


Peter Bell
Abraham “Honest Abe” Lincoln could hold his own, while also imparting knowledge and good old fashioned common sense.


George Jefferson
I feel like we should all be able to agree on the bare minimum that Barack Obama is a really talented public speaker. It really is even more obvious with the two that followed him just how well spoken he is and can come across as incredibly studious and rehearsed and then react to something that just happened and show how quick and witty he also can be at the drop of a dime. He’s also just incredibly charismatic and seemed so fucking cool which I think drew a lot of people to him especially when up against McCain and Romney.


Bill Richardson


Only one President has had generations of Americans recite a short speech written and delivered by a common man with a thin, reedy voice.
A speech which has survived so many years because of its content and elegance.
Abraham Lincoln, whose Gettysburg Address has never been surpassed in its power.
One person below has suggested that Lincoln was not a orator - but the “main event” that day was Edward Everett, renowned orator. He told Lincoln:
“I should be glad, if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion, in two hours, as you did in two minutes.”
The famed orator found Lincoln was the better orator that day. I stand by Everett’s opinion. I trust you value his opinion as well.


Todd Brooks


Of those I can remember, going back to late Eisenhower/early Kennedy, best speaker was Obama. But he was often too smart for the room. Most effective at communicating may have been Reagan, who could make people believe in fairies and leprechauns.


Sam Walker
Both Kennedy and Nixon expressed their points more clearly and respectfully than modern candidates, because at that time the strategy of zingers and other sound bites hadn’t been devised.


Bob Smith 
Yes, debates were a lot different. When I watched a tape of the Kennedy/Nixon debate, I was struck by the way Kennedy glided past an invitation to attack his opponent, but wound up calling him an "effective leader" instead:
MR. FLEMING: Senator, the Vice President in his campaign has said that you were naive and at times immature. He has raised the question of leadership. On this issue, why do you think people should vote for you rather than the Vice President?
MR. KENNEDY: Well, the Vice President and I came to the Congress together 1946; we both served in the Labor Committee. I’ve been there now for fourteen years, the same period of time that he has, so that our experience in uh – government is comparable. Secondly, I think the question is uh – what are the programs that we advocate, what is the party record that we lead? I come out of the Democratic party, which in this century has produced Woodrow Wilson and Franklin Roosevelt and Harry Truman, and which supported and sustained these programs which I’ve discussed tonight. Mr. Nixon comes out of the Republican party. He was nominated by it. And it is a fact that through most of these last twenty-five years the Republican leadership has opposed federal aid for education, medical care for the aged, development of the Tennessee Valley, development of our natural resources. I think Mr. Nixon is an effective leader of his party. I hope he would grant me the same. The question before us is: which point of view and which party do we want to lead the United States?
The effect was to completely neutralize Nixon. What could Nixon say in response without sounding petty? And how much did he want to talk about policy, once Kennedy had framed the policy debate in terms of the Democrats' most popular issues and programs?
MR. SMITH: Mr. Nixon, would you like to comment on that statement?
Mr. NIXON: I have no comment.


Clara Winters 


On the GOP side: Reagan for sure. Some of his old California Governor debates are actually even better, before he got OLD old. He used to just school gotcha journalists by how versed on facts he was.
On the Dem side: Obama at actually debating, making counterpoints, when to charge and when to hold back. Clinton at connecting with people.


Mike Rodriguez
Yeah, I agree. Obama and it’s not particularly close. As someone who was an Obama-Romney voter he routinely wiped the floor with people during debates even when he was wrong. A good example of this is him making fun of Romney for saying Russia was out biggest international foe; he made Romney look like a fool even though Romney was entirely correct.


Harry Adams
Not the President who said he has the best words. Everyone has access to all words. Spewing out a bunch of words you find impressive which have no meaning beyond just the word itself with no connected meaning-makes you like like an idiot or a jam poet, though a jam poet will probably have a means to an end.
Among the Presidents with the best words are the Rushmore Four-the three surveyors and the other guy. To this list I’d add FDR who contributed to his speeches and could be very moving when it was needed. FDR’s successor Harry Truman was about Roosevelt’s polar opposite. FDR was patrician, Harry was a former Missouri farmer, but Give ’em Hell Harry could deliver a message. JFK was a noted speaker and something of a wit. I don’t know how much of it to attribute to his chief speech writer, Ted Sorensen. Closer to the present, Barack Obama delivers amazing prepared speeches, but off the cuff as the Nation’s conscience and comforter in times of disaster, most Presidents would not be fit to hold his hat.


Maria Lopez
Hands down, former President Obama was an excellent debater and the best of the last five presidents. Obama was surgical in his debate technique, smart and quick thinking, effectively sets tone and tempo of his delivery, etc.
Former President Clinton was also a very good debater, his style was like a perfect dance where he swooned his partner who would end up agreeing to whatever he said, and whatever he wanted. Another smart president.
Former President GWB could deliver prepared speeches and debate answers very well. But if he is unprepared to answer a question, he would embarrassingly stumble:
“Rarely is the question asked, is our children learning?” —-GWB
“There’s an old saying in Tennessee, I know it’s in Texas, probably in Tennessee, that says, fool me once, shame on, shame on you. Fool me, you can’t get fooled again.”—-GWB
“One of the great things about books is sometimes there are some fantastic pictures.”—-GWB



Task:
 What president is Harry Adams talking about in his first sentence? And can you tell me how you know? Is it possible it's someone other than who it seems at first glance?

Based on the comment from Harry Adams, here is the answer to your questions.

**1. What president is Harry Adams talking about in his first sentence?**

Harry Adams is talking about **Donald Trump**.

**2. How do I know?**

I know this because the phrase "the President who said he has the best words" is a direct reference to a famous quote from Donald Trump. During the 2016 presidential campaign, Trump used this line multiple times. The most notable instance was during a debate when he said, "I went to an Ivy League college. I was a good student. I have a great vocabulary. I have the best words."

Harry Adams' subsequent criticism—that this president "spew[s] out a bunch of words you find impressive which have no meaning beyond just the word itself"—aligns with common critiques of Trump's rhetorical style, further confirming the identification.

**3. Is it possible it's someone other than who it seems at first glance?**

It is **highly unlikely** that he is referring to anyone else.

While, in a theoretical vacuum, any president *could* have uttered such a phrase, in reality, the quote "I have the best words" is uniquely and indelibly linked to Donald Trump in modern political history. No other U.S. President is known for saying this. The context of the surrounding comments, which praise the eloquence of presidents like FDR, Truman, JFK, and Obama, serves to contrast them with the president being dismissed in the opening sentence—again, pointing directly to Trump as the subject of the critique.
